newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan Taleban retreat in northern city battle.
newsitem.headline: Afghan Taleban retreat in northern city battle.

text.p: Taleban militia fighters retreated from many parts of the northern Afghan city of Mazar-i-Sharif on Wednesday after fierce battles with opposing forces, witnesses said.
A witness said at least 20 bodies of Taleban fighters lay on the ground and many vehicles had been wrecked in the clashes.
Witnesses said the purist Islamic militia had been forced out of many areas of the city and some members had been disarmed but some units remained.

The fighting erupted just after a meeting between Taleban leaders including Foreign Minister Mullah Mohammad Ghous and ethnic Uzbek General Abdul Malik, whose troops were supposed to be operating jointly with the Taleban.

Witnesses said the clashes broke out when a Taleban column of tanks and armoured personnel carriers moved into the Shi'ite northern district of Saidabad to collect weapons from suspected members of the opposition Hezb-i-Wahdat militia.
The Shi'ites fought back and were soon joined by ethnic Uzbek troops, who last week had allied with the Taleban to depose northern opposition warlord General Abdul Rashid Dostum.
The battles, which had engulfed wide areas of the city, had subsided by mid-morning, but sporadic firing and explosions could still be heard at noon.

Bursts of machinegun fire ripped through the streets and explosions from heavier weapons rocked the city through the night and into Wednesday morning. Black smoke from a burning building rose from the centre.
U.N. officials were discussing plans to evacuate international staff, but it was not immediately clear if they would be able to drive to the border with Uzbekistan or would fly to Pakistan.
Earlier on Tuesday, at least three Taleban fighters were killed by residents in Saidabad who said they were caught looting.
The Taleban arrived on Sunday, a day after Malik's soldiers captured the city and forced Dostum to flee the country.
The Islamic militia, which has not experienced street fighting in its rapid advance across Afghanistan, was now locked in combat, with its supply lines looking precarious.
Most of the Taleban's black-turbanned warriors swept in from the northwestern province of Badghis across Dostum's former territory, which may now have turned hostile.
About 200 Taleban fighters flew in on Tuesday from the southern city of Kandahar, headquarters of Taleban leader Mullah Mohammad Omar.
Malik said his revolt against Dostum was in favour of the Taleban, and his troops first rode into Mazar-i-Sharif flying white Taleban flags from their vehicles.
Tension has remained high since the Taleban's arrival, reflecting bad blood between them and the Uzbeks, many of whom fought for the communist government that collapsed in April 1992.

The United Arab Emirates on Tuesday became the third nation, after Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, to accord formal diplomatic recognition to the Taleban government, which now controls nearly 90 percent of the war-shattered country.
The United States called on Tuesday for an end to fighting in Afghanistan but left unclear whether it would accord diplomatic recognition.
